newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Thousands flee Zaire across lake to safety.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flee Zaire across lake to safety.

text.p: Pressure intensified on the United Nations and world powers to speed up a confused plan for a mission to save more than a million war refugees in Zaire.
Those lucky enough to escape continued to flee in their thousands by boat over Lake Tanganyika to the safety of neighbouring Tanzania, aid workers said on Sunday.
"Our staff in the Tanzanian port of Kigoma report an average arrival of 4,000 people a day in the area," said Jordi Riach, spokesman for the Medecins sans Frontieres charity (MSF).
The U.N. Security Council decided on Saturday to deploy a multinational force but its failure to state when or how it should go in was greeted with outrage in the humanitarian community.

Europe's top humanitarian official termed the U.N. inaction a scandal. France, which initiated the plan, pressed for early intervention, and the United States, moved by the unfolding calamity in Zaire, crawled cautiously towards action.

"We are actively studying what type of security component would be necessary for an intervention. We are also actively studying what role the U.S. might play as part of such a security component," a senior U.S. official told Reuters.
Both the United States and France are permanent members of the Security Council which gave U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali 11 days to report back to them with a "concept".

The failure to authorise immediate intervention in Zaire enraged those warning of catastrophe unless food, water and medicine is rushed to the Rwandan and Burundian refugees and east Zaireans caught up in a three-week rebellion.

"Those governments who have prevented the immediate authorisation of a multinational protection force should explain to their citizens and the world why," European Commissioner Emma Bonino thundered in Brussels.
But diplomats said the United States, Britain and Russia all had grave reservations about the French-backed plan.
"What are the intentions? What are you going to do? Who are the bad guys and how are you going to separate them from the good guys?" asked a senior diplomat in Central Africa.

In Goma, the biggest east Zaire city captured by rebels in a growing insurrection against President Mobutu Sese Seko, Red Cross officials predicted disaster and some 120 exhausted, hungry refugees arrived after walking for more than a week.
Rioting Zaireans seized the last food from a U.N. warehouse.

A German aid mission brought some hope on Saturday, delivering the first medical supplies to reach Goma since rebels captured the city just over a week ago. Ethnic Tutsi rebels have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces since October 18.

People in Goma, the target of more planned aid missions as no one else can be reached, are the fortunate ones compared to the more than a million refugees trapped on the other side of the front line, where anarchy reigns.

MSF's Riach said refugees, many of them Zaireans, joining some 26,000 who have already reached Tanzania in overcrowded and rickety old boats told of fighting and widespread looting across the lake in Fizi, south of Uvira where the rebellion began.
Local Tanzanian journalists quoted refugees as saying overloaded boats had capsized on the lake and many people were feared drowned. Immediate confirmation was not possible.

Rwanda and the rebels it supports have both rejected any French role in a multinational force, citing France's long alliances with Mobutu and with the former Rwandan Hutu leaders who ordered the genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994.
Rwanda's backing for any move to help the needy is vital. The only other corridor is through Zaire, which says the 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi must leave.
U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien apparently failed in talks in Kinshasa to persuade Zairean authorities to agree to safe havens inside Zaire for the Rwandan and Burundian refugees.
